content:
Carthage was the capital city of Ancient Carthage, on the eastern side of the Lake of Tunis in what is now Tunisia. Carthage was one of the most important trading hubs of the Mediterranean. It was one of the most affluent cities of the classical world. The city's location made it the master of maritime trade; all ships crossing the sea passed between Sicily and Tunisia, where Carthage was built, affording it great power and influence. Two large artificial harbors were built. One harbored the city's prodigious 220 warships, and the other was for trade. A walled tower overlooked both harbors. The city had massive 23-mile-long walls. Carthage was among the largest cities in preindustrial history. Whereas by 14 CE, Rome had at least 750,000 inhabitants and may have reached 1 million, the cities of Alexandria and Antioch numbered only a few hundred thousand. According to Herodian, Carthage rivaled for second place in the Roman Empire.

Carthage developed from a Canaanite Phoenician colony into the capital of a Punic empire. The city dominated large parts of the Mediterranean during the first millennium BCE. The legendary Queen Alyssa or Dido is regarded as its founder. In most accounts, she was the queen of the Phoenician city-state of Tyre (today in Lebanon). Dido is described as a clever and enterprising woman who fled her ruthless and autocratic brother, Pygmalion. She had discovered that he was responsible for her husband's death. She fled tyranny to found her own city. Through her wisdom and leadership, Carthage prospered. According to Timaeus of Tauromenium, she purchased the land from a local tribe. They agreed she could buy what could be covered by an oxhide. Dido cut the oxhide into fine strips so that she had enough to encircle an entire nearby hill. That would become their new home.

The Carthaginian republic became one of the longest-lived and largest states in the ancient Mediterranean. The founders were Phoenician settlers from the Near East. They spoke Canaanite, a Semitic language, and followed a local variety of the ancient Punic religion. They traveled widely by sea and set up many colonies. Carthage differed from Greek, Phoenician, and Tyrian colonizers who "only required colonies to pay due respect for their home cities." Carthage "sent its own leaders to govern colonies." Back home, Punic Carthage was divided into four equally sized residential areas with the same layout. The city had religious areas, marketplaces, a council house, towers, a theater, and a huge necropolis. In the middle of the city stood a high fortress called the Byrsa. By the eighth century, fabric dyeing efforts had started. This is evident from crushed shells of murex snails (from which “royal purple” was derived).

The First Punic War (264–241 BCE) was the first of three wars fought between Rome and Carthage, the two main powers of the western Mediterranean. For 23 years, in the longest continuous conflict and greatest naval war of antiquity, the two powers struggled for supremacy. Then, Carthage and Rome fought the 17-year-long Second Punic War between 218 and 201 BCE, ending with a Roman victory. The peace treaty stripped Carthage of all of its overseas and some of its African territories. A huge monetary fine was to be paid over 50 years. Hostages were taken. Carthage was forbidden to possess war elephants. Its fleet was restricted to 10 warships. It was prohibited from waging war outside Africa and in Africa only with Rome's express permission. Many senior Carthaginians wanted to reject it, but Hannibal spoke strongly in its favor, and it was accepted in the spring of 201 BCE. Henceforth, Carthage was politically subordinate to Rome.
